strengths: Novel and interesting theoretical framing: connects the well-established but under-explored Pi-Noise (positive-incentive noise) framework to contrastive learning by defining a task entropy via an auxiliary Gaussian distribution tied to the contrastive loss, and shows that standard predefined augmentations can be interpreted as a point-estimate of this beneficial noise.

Broad empirical validation: experiments span 5 non-vision datasets (HAR, Reuters, Reuters-21578, Epsilon, MSLR-WEB30K) and 5 vision datasets (CIFAR-10/100, Fashion-MNIST, STL-10, ImageNet), and the method is tested as a plug-in on many base contrastive frameworks (SimCLR, MoCo, BYOL, SimSiam, DINO), demonstrating broad compatibility.

Practically useful direction: the proposed generator does not depend on data modality, offering a principled alternative to hand-crafted augmentations for non-vision data where designing good augmentations is notoriously hard.

Extensive ablations covering noise distribution family (Gaussian vs. uniform), generator architecture (DNN/ResNet18/ResNet50/U-Net), batch size sensitivity, comparison against SAM-based background segmentation, and computational overhead analysis (time/FLOPs/memory), giving a fairly complete picture of the method's costs and behavior.

Qualitative visualizations (Figures 1, 4, 6, 7) are compelling and suggest the learned noise captures semantically meaningful structure (foreground/background separation), providing some intuitive support for the theoretical claims.
weaknesses: The core theoretical derivation is somewhat post-hoc: the auxiliary Gaussian distribution used to define task entropy is essentially designed to reproduce the existing contrastive loss (Eq. 6-8), so the subsequent 'proof' that predefined augmentation equals a point estimate of pi-noise largely restates that MAP estimation is a special case of a distributional formulation — a fairly standard/near-tautological observation rather than a deep new insight, which weakens the novelty claim relative to its heavy notation.

Many reported improvements are numerically small (often <1-2 points) with overlapping or comparable standard deviations across multiple runs (e.g., Table 3, Table 4), raising concerns about the statistical robustness of the claimed gains, especially given the very large number of comparisons made across tables without correction for multiple comparisons.

Baselines are trained under resource-constrained settings (reduced batch size, fewer epochs, e.g., ImageNet only trained for 100 epochs, SimCLR batch sizes far below the original 4096) that are known to be far from these methods' optimal operating regimes; this makes it hard to assess whether PiNDA's benefits persist when baselines are properly tuned/scaled, undermining the significance claims.

PiNDA introduces a full secondary neural network (often the same architecture as the backbone) as the noise generator, roughly doubling FLOPs/memory/time in several settings (Tables 6, 9, 10); the paper's attempt to show this is 'worth it' compared to simply increasing batch size (Table 11) is based on only two limited experiments and not a comprehensive cost-controlled study.

Some implementation details relevant to reproducibility (e.g., the extra penalty term on noise norm mentioned only briefly in Appendix B.4, its weighting, and its necessity/effect) are not integrated into the main theoretical framework, suggesting the practical method relies on ad hoc engineering choices beyond what the theory derives.

The interpretation of visualizations (e.g., 'style transfer'-like effects, background/foreground separation) is largely qualitative/anecdotal; no quantitative metric is used to substantiate that the learned noise constitutes semantically meaningful or superior augmentations beyond downstream accuracy.

Some baselines used for comparison (SimCL, CLAE) show very large variances across runs (e.g., std >3-6% in Table 2), which weakens their reliability as a point of comparison and makes relative improvement claims less convincing.

strengths: The paper proposes an interesting theoretical bridge between the π-noise framework and contrastive learning by constructing an auxiliary Gaussian distribution tied to the contrastive loss, offering a fresh perspective on why data augmentation matters in contrastive learning.

The experimental scope is broad, covering 5 non-vision and 5 vision datasets, multiple contrastive backbones (SimCLR, BYOL, SimSiam, MoCo, DINO), and several noise-generator architectures (ResNet18/50, U-Net).
The method is presented as a plug-and-play module compatible with existing contrastive frameworks, which is a practically appealing design choice.
The visualizations (Figs. 1, 4, 6, 7) are intriguing, suggesting the learned π-noise focuses on background/context regions rather than the main object, which is a qualitatively interesting finding.
Extensive ablations are provided (noise-generator choice, batch size, comparison with SAM-based masking, computational cost breakdown), showing effort toward thorough empirical validation.
weaknesses: The central theoretical claim that predefined data augmentation is a 'point estimation' of π-noise is essentially a restatement: setting p(ε|x) to a Dirac delta (Eq. 12) is simply the definition of using a fixed, non-learned augmentation, not a deep or novel theoretical insight, despite being framed as one of the main contributions.

The auxiliary Gaussian distribution (Eqs. 6-8) used to define task entropy appears to be reverse-engineered to force contrastive learning into the π-noise formalism (max MI(T,E)) rather than derived from first principles; the choice of Gaussian form and the specific mapping γθ*(x)→variance is not well motivated beyond mathematical convenience.

The derivation is circular in practice: the theory relies on the 'optimal' parameters θ*, but the paper simply substitutes the current (non-optimal) θ during training (Section 3.3-3.4) without justifying why this substitution preserves the claimed mutual-information-maximization properties.

Baseline reproduction is weak and undermines the empirical comparisons: the authors admit SimCLR and other baselines cannot reach published accuracy levels (e.g., 86% vs >90%+ typically reported for CIFAR-10) due to batch-size limitations, which calls into question whether the reported relative improvements from PiNDA are due to the method itself or simply noise/variance in an already degraded baseline.

Reported improvements from PiNDA are frequently marginal (often <1-2 points, and within one standard deviation of the baseline in several tables, e.g., Table 3, Table 4 BYOL/SimSiam rows), while the method introduces non-trivial extra computational cost (Tables 9-10 show up to +20-133GB memory and substantial FLOPs increase), raising concerns about the practical cost-benefit tradeoff.

Results across different noise parameterizations (N(0,Σ) vs N(μ,Σ) vs uniform) are inconsistent across datasets/models with no principled explanation for when each should be used, weakening the claim that the theoretical framework provides actionable, general guidance (e.g., the recommendation to fix μ=0 is purely empirical, not derived from the theory).

Evaluation relies only on kNN and a simple softmax-regression probe rather than standard linear-evaluation protocols widely used in contrastive learning papers, making it harder to compare against the broader literature and assess representation quality rigorously.

The noise-generator architecture ablation (Table 6) shows contradictory trends (e.g., ResNet50 generator sometimes substantially hurts performance relative to the no-augmentation baseline, e.g., 54.72 vs 61.69 kNN on STL-10), suggesting the method's effectiveness is sensitive to implementation choices in ways not well explained or controlled for.

The qualitative claims about the noise generator learning 'style-transfer'-like or object-aware augmentations are largely anecdotal, based on visual inspection of a handful of examples, without quantitative analysis (e.g., saliency correlation, segmentation overlap metrics) to substantiate the interpretive claims.

strengths: The paper establishes an interesting conceptual bridge between the π-noise framework and contrastive learning by constructing an auxiliary Gaussian distribution from the contrastive loss, giving a principled (if heuristic) way to define 'task entropy' without labels, which is a reasonable extension of prior π-noise work that relied on supervised label distributions.
The theoretical narrative (standard augmentations = point estimation of π-noise; learning π-noise generalizes this) is intuitive and provides a clear motivation for the proposed PiNDA method.

Extensive empirical evaluation across 5 non-vision and 5 vision datasets, and compatibility demonstrated with many contrastive frameworks (SimCLR, MoCo, BYOL, SimSiam, DINO), showing the method is a plug-in module rather than a standalone architecture.

Thorough ablations: noise distribution family (Gaussian vs uniform), fixing vs learning the mean, different noise-generator architectures (ResNet18/50, U-Net), batch-size sensitivity, additional computational cost accounting, and a comparison against a SAM-based background-noise heuristic.

The visualizations (Figures 1, 4, 6, 7) are a genuinely interesting qualitative result, showing the learned noise concentrates on background/context regions and resembles style-transfer-like augmentations, which supports the paper's central intuition in an intuitive, inspectable way.
Reasonable attention to reproducibility burden, including reporting FLOPs/time/memory overhead and convergence curves in the appendix.
weaknesses: The theoretical construction is more of a reinterpretation than a rigorous derivation: the mapping from contrastive loss to an auxiliary Gaussian entropy (Eq. 6-8) is one arbitrary choice among many possible monotone transforms, and the paper itself admits the specific functional form does not affect the conclusion, which undercuts the claim that this 'properly defines' task entropy rather than simply providing a convenient proxy.

The point-estimation argument (Eq. 12, MAP-style Dirac delta assumption) essentially re-derives the standard InfoNCE objective by construction, so the 'proof' that existing augmentations are point estimates of π-noise is somewhat tautological rather than a novel technical insight with predictive power beyond motivating the follow-up algorithm.

Empirical gains are frequently small and inconsistent across settings (e.g., BYOL/SimSiam/MoCo on ImageNet or CIFAR often improve by well under 1 point, some within one standard deviation of the baseline), while a few cases (SimCLR on ImageNet, SimSiam on STL-10) show large jumps with no analysis of why the benefit is so architecture- or dataset-dependent.

Baseline numbers are acknowledged to be far below published results due to compute-limited batch sizes (e.g., SimCLR at batch size 64/256/512 instead of the thousands used in the original paper), which weakens the reliability of absolute and possibly relative comparisons, since sensitivity to batch size is well known to be nonlinear for contrastive methods.

Practical implementation deviates from the clean theory: an extra ad hoc penalty term (inverse norm of the noise) is added to the vision loss to prevent noise collapse, which is not derived from or predicted by the theoretical framework, suggesting the theory under-specifies practical necessities.

The SAM comparison is a somewhat weak strawman (an expensive, non-learned heuristic segmentation-based noise injection) rather than a comparison against more sophisticated learned-augmentation baselines (e.g., learned RandAugment/AutoAugment policies, adversarial augmentation search), limiting the strength of the significance claims.

Presentation is dense with heavy notation and the practical algorithm (Alg. 1/2) leaves some ambiguities, e.g., how θ* (the 'optimal' parameters) is operationalized during training (current θ is used, not a true optimum), which is glossed over.

No statistical significance testing or discussion of when/why improvements are expected to be large vs negligible; the paper would benefit from a clearer characterization of the conditions under which PiNDA is expected to help versus provide marginal benefit.
